Welcome toA Flash in a Long Bar

A flash heats one thin slice of a long bar: how does the heat spread, and how fast?

Listen to the intro

About: the heat kernel: heat released in a thin slice of an infinite insulated bar spreading by conduction

About this simulation

On screen
The temperature T against x along the bar, x from −20 to 20 cm and T from 0 to 6 K. The orange curve is the current time, with a short horizontal bar marking ±σ at e−1/2 of its peak. The bar itself is drawn under the x-axis, tinted by its temperature, with a thermometer standing on it at xp. Optional blue curves show the three Figure 68 snapshots at t1 = 1 s (solid), t2 = 4 s (dashed) and t3 = 16 s (dotted). The inset, upper right, plots the thermometer reading against time from 1 to 64 s, on a linear scale fitted to that thermometer's largest reading.
Controls
The time slider sets the time since the flash, 1 to 64 s; the buttons under it set 1, 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64 s exactly. The ×4 button multiplies the time by four, up to t = 16 s. The thermometer slider moves it 2 to 16 cm from the slice. The Snapshots switch adds the three curves of Figure 68 in the notes.
Measured
All temperatures come from the exact Gaussian solution with D = 1.0 cm2/s and ℰ/ρc = 20 K cm. σ = √(2Dt) is the width, and the area is the integral of T over the whole bar.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Four times the time

Set t = 1 s, with the thermometer at 2 cm and the snapshots hidden; the curve is 5.64 K high with a width σ = 1.41 cm. Before pressing the button that multiplies the time by four, predict the curve at t = 4 s.

2 · The area under the curve

Keep t = 4 s and switch on the snapshots at 1, 4 and 16 s, which are 5.64 K, 2.82 K and 1.41 K high. At t = 1 s the area under the curve is 20.0 K cm. Before pressing the button that multiplies the time by four, predict the area under the curve at t = 16 s. Then press it.

3 · Just after the flash

Keep the snapshots on and set t = 1 s, the earliest time on the slider. Before comparing the three curves, predict what the curve becomes as the time since the flash is made shorter and shorter than 1 s.

4 · A thermometer far away

Set t = 1 s, switch off the snapshots, and keep the thermometer at 2 cm. Before moving it to 16 cm, where the orange curve looks flat on the axis, predict its temperature rise there. Then move it.

5 · Moving the thermometer out

Move the thermometer to 4 cm and set t = 8 s; the inset shows its reading rising to a largest value of 1.21 K at 8 s and falling after that. The buttons under the time slider set exact times. Before moving the thermometer to 8 cm, predict when its reading will be largest.

6 · Summary

Heat released in a thin slice spreads as a Gaussian, T = (ℰ/ρc) e−x²/4Dt/√(4πDt), the heat kernel. Its width grows as σ = √(2Dt), its peak falls as 1/√t, and its area, the total heat, never changes. It is positive at every distance at once, and a point at distance x warms most at t = x2/2D.

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A brief flash of light heats a thin slice in the middle of a long insulated bar. This sim draws the temperature along the bar a time t after the flash, with a thermometer that reads it at one chosen distance.

What you'll learn

  • What temperature curve a single flash of heat leaves in a long bar.
  • How the curve and its area change as time passes.
  • What a thermometer at a fixed distance reads over time.
The sim's layout at t = 1 s. The inset is shown empty here.

What's on screen

  • The orange curve: the temperature T along the bar, x from −20 to 20 cm, at the time you set, with a black bar marking ±σ. The bar is drawn under the axis, tinted by temperature, with the thermometer on it.
  • Blue curves, if switched on: snapshots at 1 s (solid), 4 s (dashed) and 16 s (dotted).
  • Inset, upper right: the thermometer reading against time, 1 to 64 s, with a dot at the present time.
See itLook at the opening state: t = 1 s, the thermometer at 2 cm, no snapshots. Watch for: the orange curve, the ±σ bar, the thermometer on the tinted bar and the inset in the corner.

Fixed: D = 1.0 cm2/s and ℰ/ρc = 20 K cm. Every temperature comes from the exact Gaussian solution, not from a simulation of heat moving.

03

A flash of heat spreads as a Gaussian

Heat ℰ per unit area is released at t = 0 in a thin slice at x = 0, so the bar starts with T = (ℰ/ρc) δ(x). The bar is insulated and long enough to count as infinite. The temperature afterwards is the heat kernel, the notes' (7.59):

The notes' (7.59), with the thin-slice initial temperature.

In the sim D = 1.0 cm2/s and ℰ/ρc = 20 K cm. The curve is a Gaussian centred on the slice. Its peak is T(0, t) = 20 K cm/√(4πDt), which is 5.64 K at t = 1 s.

The black bar of the sim spans ±σ, where σ = √(2Dt) is the distance at which the curve has fallen to e−1/2 of its peak. At 1 s, σ = 1.41 cm and the curve there is 3.42 K.

Key idea. One flash leaves a Gaussian centred on the slice, with a width σ = √(2Dt) set by the time since the flash.
The curve at t = 1 s, with the peak and the ±σ bar the sim draws.
See itLook at t = 1 s, with the thermometer at 2 cm. Watch for: the peak at 5.64 K and the ±σ bar 1.41 cm to each side, at 3.42 K.
04

Four times the time doubles the width and halves the height

Time enters only through the product Dt. Since σ = √(2Dt), multiplying t by four multiplies σ by √4 = 2. The peak goes as 1/√t, so it falls to half. Figure 68 of the notes draws the curve at t1, t2 = 4t1 and t3 = 16t1:

The width and the peak, from (7.59).

With t1 = 1 s the sim gives 5.64 K and σ = 1.41 cm, then 2.82 K and 2.83 cm at 4 s, then 1.41 K and 5.66 cm at 16 s. A warm region moving at a steady speed would have four times the width at 4 s. Diffusion spreads as √t, which is slower than that.

Key idea. Each time t is multiplied by four, the Gaussian becomes twice as wide and half as tall.
The three snapshots of Figure 68, as the sim draws them with the switch on.
See itSet t = 4 s with the snapshots on. Watch for: the orange curve lying on the dashed one, 2.82 K high, with σ = 2.83 cm.
See itSet t = 16 s with the snapshots on. Watch for: the orange curve on the dotted one, 1.41 K high and σ = 5.66 cm.
05

The area is fixed, so an earlier time is a taller spike

The heat per unit area in the bar is ∫ρcT dx. The Gaussian integral of Section 2.3 gives ℰ at every time, as conservation of heat requires:

Conservation of heat.

The sim shows ∫T dx = 20.0 K cm at 1, 4 and 16 s. The peak falls only because the heat spreads: peak × σ × √(2π) = 5.64 K × 1.41 cm × 2.51 = 20.0 K cm. Nothing leaves the insulated bar.

Going earlier works the same way backwards. At 1/4 s the peak is 11.3 K and σ = 0.71 cm; at 1/16 s, 22.6 K and 0.35 cm. As t → 0 the curve tends to a delta function, the one of Section 6.3:

The limit of (7.59), the delta function of an ideal thin slice.
Key idea. The area ℰ/ρc stays 20.0 K cm, so as t shrinks the curve gets narrower and taller without limit.
Times earlier than the slider reaches. Each curve encloses 20.0 K cm.
See itSet t = 16 s with the snapshots on, and read the area. Watch for: ∫T dx still 20.0 K cm, though the peak is a quarter of what it was at 1 s.
See itSet t = 1 s, the earliest the slider reaches, with the snapshots on. Watch for: the t₁ curve narrowest and tallest, with the area at 20.0 K cm.
06

Every distance warms at once

The factor e−x²/4Dt is positive at every x for every t > 0. Fourier's law makes the heat flux respond at once to the temperature gradient, so heat has no front that has to arrive. A disturbance on a string reaches x only after a time x/v.

The rise is tiny far away. At t = 1 s, T = 5.64 K × e−x²/4: it is 2.08 K at 2 cm, 0.103 K at 4 cm, 6.35 × 10−7 K at 8 cm, and at 16 cm the factor is e−64, so T = 9.05 × 10−28 K.

That is far below anything measurable, and the orange curve looks flat on the axis there. It is still positive, and it is never negative.

T at t = 1 s on a logarithmic scale. Zero would lie at minus infinity, below the chart.
Key idea. In this model heat has no finite speed: the temperature is positive everywhere at every t > 0.
See itSet t = 1 s and move the thermometer to 16 cm. Watch for: the reading T(xp, t) of 9.05 × 10⁻²⁸ K, though the curve looks flat there.
07

A point is warmest at t = x²/2D

At a fixed distance x the reading rises, while the curve is still widening towards x, and then falls, as the peak drops. It is largest when ∂T/∂t = 0, which gives t = x²/2D. At that moment σ = x, so the thermometer sits at the end of the ±σ bar.

From ∂T/∂t = 0 in (7.59).

The largest reading is therefore e−1/2 times the peak of the whole curve, and it falls as 1/x. At 4 cm it is 1.21 K at 8 s. At 8 cm it is 0.605 K at 32 s.

Twice the distance means four times the time: the warmest moment goes as x², not as x. At 16 cm it would be at 128 s, beyond the slider's end.

08

Where it matters

  • Measuring diffusivity. A brief flash on a sample, and the time at which a thermometer at distance x reads highest, give D = x²/2tmax in this model.
  • Spreading of anything that diffuses. Ink in water, a dopant in a crystal or a smell in a still room spread with σ = √(2Dt). Doubling the width takes four times as long.
  • Any starting profile. The temperature is the kernel convolved with the initial temperature, so any start is a sum of flashes (the notes, Section 7.3).
  • Waves differ. A pulse on a string arrives after x/v, while the kernel is positive at once everywhere. The kernel is a model, not a statement that a signal is instant.
09

Summary

In one line. This sim shows how heat released in one thin slice of a long bar spreads along it.
  • T = (ℰ/ρc) e−x²/4Dt/√(4πDt): a Gaussian with σ = √(2Dt) and a peak that falls as 1/√t.
  • Four times the time makes it twice as wide and half as tall, with the area fixed at ℰ/ρc = 20.0 K cm.
  • It is positive at every distance at once, and a point at x is warmest at t = x²/2D.

Common mix-ups

  • "The warm region spreads at a steady speed." Four times the time only doubles the width.
  • "A falling peak means heat has left." The area stays 20.0 K cm.
  • "Beyond the curve the temperature is zero." At 16 cm after 1 s it is 9.05 × 10⁻²⁸ K: tiny, not zero, never negative.
  • "Twice as far means twice as late." The warmest moment goes as x²: 8 s at 4 cm, 32 s at 8 cm.

Things to try on your own

  • Press × 4 time three times from 1 s and watch σ and the peak at each step.
  • Set t = x²/2 for an xp and check that the reading is the largest on its inset curve.
